strands.subStrand: Listening for information   Gender roles  Responding to questions
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify gender roles from aural texts for information, b) respond to questions on gender roles in the community from texts for comprehension, c) recognise the importance of listening purposefully for comprehension.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  collaborate with peers to hold a discussion forum on gender roles in communities,  listen to a recording or talk on the theme,  identify vocabulary related to the theme,  prepare a vocabulary list with the words related to the theme,  work with peers to identify the meaning of new words and words related to them (e.g. synonyms and opposites)  make simple sentences using the vocabulary identified,  answer direct and inferential questions from a text related to the theme,  work collaboratively to conduct
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How do we listen to get information from an aural text? 2. Why should some opportunities be equal among both girls and boys?

strands.subStrand: Reading for comprehension   Vocabulary  Direct and inferential questions  Tense- present and past tense
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) answer questions from texts related to the theme for comprehension, b) use the vocabulary on the theme to construct sentences in appropriate tenses for communication, c) embrace the use of interpersonal skills to enhance positive gender roles in society.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  conduct a reader’s theatre to read texts related to the theme,  work with peers to identify vocabulary related to the theme,  answer direct and inferential questions from the texts,  work with peers to discuss how action (verbs) can be described in their present and past tense,  work as a class to create a table to differentiate between verbs in their present and past tense,  display the table on the language corner and take turns to read,  make sentences using the verbs in their present and past tense,  use substitution tables to makes sentences related to the theme,  share their sentences with peers for peer review.
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How can we differentiate between actions done in the past and in the present? 2. Why is it important to apply comprehension skills in reading?

strands.subStrand: Essay writing – Expository essay
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) research on an issue related to the theme for information, b) write an expository essay on gender roles for effective communication, c) embrace the importance of organising ideas into a coherent sequence for communication.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  work with peers to carry out a research on an issue related to the theme,  make notes on their findings,  work with peers to brainstorm and write an outline of an expository essay on the theme,  create a vocabulary bank using the vocabulary picked,  collaborate with peers to sort flashcards with ideas on gender roles in the community,  organise the ideas on the gender roles into a coherent sequence,  construct paragraphs from the ideas on the cards and sequence them into a meaningful expository essay,  edit and review the essay for coherence and effective communication,
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How do we organise information logically in writing? 2. Why is it important to understand gender roles in the community?

strands.subStrand: Listening for comprehension   The internet  Tense- future tense
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) outline the advantages and disadvantages of the internet for information, b) identify future tense from aural texts for information, c) value the importance of listening attentively as a way of acquiring information.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  brainstorm the uses and dangers of the internet with peers,  list on separate charts the advantages and disadvantages of the internet and display in class,  listen to a passage on the proper use of the internet and take notes,  discuss the do’s and don’ts of the use of the internet with peers,  create a glossary of new words related to the theme from the text listened to,  conduct a discussion on how to describe actions in future tense,
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How do we listen to acquire information? 2. Why is it important to observe netiquette when using the internet?

strands.subStrand: Extensive reading – Library skills   Tracing resources  Tracking reading progress  Tense- future tense
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) trace specific reading materials from online or print sources, b) track their reading progress by creating a reading log, c) embrace safe use of the internet as a source of information for lifelong learning
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  search for texts related to technology, social media or the internet, using digital devices or the library,  collaborate with peers to conduct a silent reading session,  list down the vocabulary identified from the read texts,  pick out names of digital devices from the texts read and write them on charts for display,  prepare a reading log on the resources read including key details (e.g. title, author, main idea, vocabulary),  identify sentences written in future tense and note them down,  create a reading club with peers and exchange reading resources.
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How do we get information on something we want to understand more? 2. Why is it important to use the internet safely and cautiously?

strands.subStrand: Social writing – Cards   Invitation card  Appreciation card  Congratulatory card
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify the key components of a card for information, b) design a card (invitation card, appreciation card, congratulatory card) for effective communication, c) advocate for the role of social writing in enhancing communication.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  work with peers to collect sample cards from online and print sources,  study the cards to identify the key message passed,  identify the features of the cards,  work with peers to design a thank you card, congratulatory card and invitation card,  display the cards in the class gallery for peer review,  use a digital device to create a variety of e-cards (invitation, appreciation, congratulatory cards),  present the designed e-cards to the class for peer review.
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. Why do we present cards to people? 2. How can we make cards more appealing when designing them?

strands.subStrand: Attentive listening   Common conversation al errors  Responding to questions
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify common conversational errors for information, b) respond to questions from an aural text for comprehension, c) acknowledge the role of conversational skills in day-to-day communication.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  discuss with peers common conversational errors among speakers,  listen to a conversation on human-wildlife conflict between a game warden and a farmer (complaining about wild animals destroying crops in his or her farm),  identify conversational errors that may be as a result of poor turn- taking and interrupting impolitely,  role play the conversation again while correcting the conversational errors made,  respond to questions from texts.
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. Why is it important to interrupt politely in a conversation? 2. How do we avoid conflict with wild animals?

strands.subStrand: Extensive Reading  Grade Appropriate Texts  Vocabulary building  Paraphrasing main idea
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) explain vocabulary related to the theme for effective communication, b) paraphrase the main idea from a text for comprehension, c) embrace reading as a source of acquiring information.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  read texts related safety of wild animals on our roads (for example, road signs, being cautious, animal ambulance),  identify vocabulary related to the theme- wildlife,  team up with peers to play a language game to match the vocabulary identified to their meaning,  work with peers to construct sentences using the vocabulary identified,  paraphrase the main idea from the text,  share the summary with peers for review,  collaborate with peers to prepare a creative mosaic of a wild animal of choice and display during the interclass festival.
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. Why should we read extensively? 2. Why is it important to take care of wildlife? 3. What can be done to avoid road clashes involving wild animals?

strands.subStrand: Writing for information – Paragraph writing
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify the features of a well-developed paragraph, b) compose two well sequenced paragraphs on the theme for information, c) acknowledge writing as a channel for addressing pertinent issues and ideas.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  brainstorm with peers the features of a well-developed paragraph,  work with peers to study a collection of paragraphs,  collaborate with peers to review the paragraphs and identify whether they are well developed and written,  prepare a sketch of ideas related to the theme,  use the sketched ideas to compose a paragraph on the theme,  share their paragraphs with peers for review,  display the best written paragraphs in the class gallery,  conduct a writing contest to identify well developed paragraphs from the class.
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How do we write paragraphs? 2. Why is it important to preserve wildlife?

strands.subStrand: Public speaking – Impromptu speech  Non-verbal cues
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify the non-verbal cues in communication, b) present a short talk on the theme using appropriate non-verbal cues for effective communication, c) recognise the value of non-verbal cues in enhancing communication.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  watch and listen to a video recording of a story on safety at school,  identify the non-verbal cues (e.g. gestures, facial expressions, movement) used in presentation of the story,  discuss how the cues help to enhance understanding in speaking,  present the short talk using appropriate non-verbal cues at a class assembly or during club activities,  visit an institution that provides first aid services (hospital, the Red Cross, St. John’s Ambulance or the Kenya Police) and listen keenly to
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How do non- verbal cues enhance understanding? 2. Why is it important to follow the appropriate steps of first aid in case of an accident?

strands.subStrand: Reading for information – Poetry   Responding to questions  Vocabulary building  Sentence construction
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) respond to questions from texts for information, b) create a glossary with words related to the theme for information, c) construct sentence using the new vocabulary for effective communication, d) appreciate the role of reading as a way of acquiring information.

strands.subStrand: Writing to give information   Connectors of sequence  Composition writing
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) outline the steps of responding to an emergency in school, b) write a composition on the process of responding to an emergency in school, c) recognise process writing as a way of passing information.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  watch a short video or read a passage on the process of responding to an emergency,  work with peers to summarise what happens in the video or passage,  outline the main steps taken in responding to the emergency in the video or passage,  compile a list of connectors of sequence used to sequence ideas in paragraphs (e.g. first, second, then, finally)  write a composition laying out the process of responding to an emergency based on the main steps outlined using the connectors of sequence,  present the composition to other members of class for peer review,  organise their best compositions in
strands.inquiryQuestions: Why is it important to understand how to respond to an emergency?

strands.subStrand: Storytelling   Proverbs and wise sayings  Re-telling stories  Lessons learnt
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) re-tell a short story on the theme for expression, b) explain proverbs and wise sayings used in oral presentations for information, c) embrace the common community values for lifelong learning.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  listen to a story from a good narrator or a digital or electronic device on the African community values (respect, unity and hard work),  discuss the lessons learnt from the story,  identify the features that made the story telling session interesting,  work with peers to put together a collection of proverbs and wise sayings,  discuss the meaning of the proverbs and wise sayings,  write the proverbs and wise sayings on sentence strips and display them in class,  create a proverbs and sayings
strands.inquiryQuestions: Why is it important to pass culture from one generation to another?

strands.subStrand: Reading for information   Vocabulary building  Responding to questions
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify vocabulary related to the theme for information, b) respond to questions from texts for comprehension, c) acknowledge the role of reading for acquisition of information.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  surf the internet or read books with texts related to the theme,  identify meaning of vocabulary in the texts,  answer direct and inferential questions from the texts,  make a summary of the key ideas from the texts,  identify specific details from the texts (e.g. characters, vocabulary)  discuss the importance of each of the values mentioned from the context of the text,  prepare a skit on community values and roleplay during club activities or school events.
strands.inquiryQuestions: Why are community values important?

strands.subStrand: Creative writing – Poetry   Features of poems  Aspects of style
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify features of a poem for information, b) write a simple poem on the theme for creative expression, c) advocate for the use of poetry in the promotion of community values.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  work collaboratively to discuss aspects of poetry (e.g. theme, diction, line, stanza, imagery and persona),  watch a presentation of or read a simple poem on the theme,  explain the main message from the poem,  identify aspects of style (e.g. repetition, rhyme, imagery, symbolism, and rhythm),  compose simple poems on community values,  recite the verses for peer review,  discuss how language is used in poetry,  compare language use in poetry with ordinary language.
strands.inquiryQuestions: Why are poems important in transmitting culture?

strands.subStrand: Self-expression – interviews   Characteristics of a good presentation  Audience awareness  Turn taking and interrupting politely
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify the characteristics of a good oral presentation for information, b) apply audience awareness in a mock interview session for expression, c) observe the skills of turn- taking and interrupting politely in a dialogue for expression, d) value the need for confidence in oral presentation for self- expression.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  work with peers to listen to a recording of an interview panel on the theme,  identify vocabulary used in the interview,  work in partnership with peers to find out the meaning of the new words identified,  conduct a mock interview with peers on a topic related to the theme,  apply turn taking and interrupting politely in the mock interview,  peer review peers’ performance,  discuss with peers on effects of poor turn taking
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How do we apply audience awareness in public speaking? 2. Why is it important to take turns and interrupt politely in dialogues?

strands.subStrand: Reading for comprehension – Play   Vocabulary building  Summarising main ideas  Responding to questions
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify vocabulary on indigenous trade from a play for information, b) summarise the main ideas from a play for comprehension, c) respond to questions from a play for comprehension, d) acknowledge relating events and ideas to real life for life-long learning.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  conduct a reader’s theatre to read an excerpt of a play on indigenous languages,  identify vocabulary related to indigenous trade from the plays read,  conduct a spelling bee mini- contest to spell out and read the vocabulary related to the theme,  work together to match the new words to their meaning,  make notes on the key details from the play,  team up to discuss the characteristics of a play with examples from the plays read,  write down a summary of the main events from the plays,  answer direct and inferential questions from the plays,  role-play a skit on an
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How can we enhance comprehension when reading a play? 2. How does indigenous trade differ from modern trade?

strands.subStrand: Writing to give information – Dialogue
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) examine the features of a dialogue for effective writing, b) create a dialogue on the theme for information, c) acknowledge the importance of dialogue writing in communication.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  collaborate with peers to discuss the features of a dialogue,  role play a dialogue with peers on a topic related to the theme of indigenous trade,  sketch an outline of a simple dialogue on a topic related to the theme,  share their sketch with peers for review,  compose the dialogue based on the reviewed outline,  exchange their dialogues with peers and identify the main ideas in the dialogues,  organise their well written dialogues in the class portfolio.
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. What are the key features of a dialogue? 2. Why are values important when engaging in any business transaction?

strands.subStrand: Presentation skills – Debate   Vocabulary  Organizing ideas logically  Audience awareness skills
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify vocabulary related to sports and games for information, b) organise ideas logically for communication for comprehension, c) apply appropriate audience awareness skills during debate for expression, d) acknowledge audience awareness skills in effective public presentations.
strands.experiences: By the end of the Sub

strands.subStrand: Reading for information   Responding to questions  Vocabulary building  Summarising ideas
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) answer questions from texts for information, b) create a personal collection of vocabulary related to the theme for comprehension, c) summarise the key ideas from texts for information, d) embrace the acquisition of knowledge on sports and games through reading.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  search from online and offline sources for short passages on sports and games,  conduct a silent reading session to read short passages related to the theme,  answer direct and inferential questions on the short passages read,  work collaboratively to prepare flashcards with the vocabulary identified from the passage,  display the flashcards for peers to read aloud,  make notes on the main ideas from texts.
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How do we read to find information from texts efficiently? 2. Why should we engage in sports and games?

strands.subStrand: Essay writing – Descriptive composition   Descriptive composition  Adjectives
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify descriptive words from a text on sports and games, b) write a descriptive composition on a topic related to the theme for information, c) advocate for use of appropriate descriptive words in communication.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  read a text on sports and games from online or print sources,  collaborate with peers to identify descriptive words (adjectives) as used in the text,  take turns to play a language game where they describe an object using non-verbal cues and have their peers guess what object it is,  write an outline of a descriptive composition on a sport or game of their choice,  make a list of words that can be used to describe things, people, events or feelings related to the sport or game,  write a composition (240 – 280 words) describing a sport or game of choice,  share their composition with peers for review,  conduct a writing contest to establish the best descriptive
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How do we present information in descriptive writing? 2. Why is it important to consider personal interests when choosing a sport or game?

strands.subStrand: Story telling – Ogre narrative   Characteristics of a good storyteller  Moral lessons
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) explain the characteristics of a good story teller for information, b) retell an ogre narrative from the community for effective communication, c) acknowledge the role of ogre narratives in the preservation of culture.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  work with peers to collect a variety of ogre stories from the community and organize in a class portfolio,  collaborate with peers to identify features that make a story telling session interesting (e.g. gestures, audience involvement, tonal variation, dramatization),  work with peers to draw ogres based on their mental perception,  team up to prepare traditional attire, ornaments or instruments that can be used in a storytelling session,  take turns to conduct a story telling session on ogre stories from African communities,  work jointly to record the story telling session,
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. Why are ogre stories important? 2. How can we make a storytelling session more captivating?

strands.subStrand: Intensive reading – Ogre stories   Features  Responding to questions  Vocabulary building
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify the features of ogre stories for information, b) respond to questions from texts for comprehension, c) use vocabulary related to the theme in sentence construction for comprehension, d) embrace the place of ogre tales in cultural conservation.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  listen to ogre tales from a resource person,  team up to identify the features of ogre stories,  present the features discussed for peer review,  collaborate with peers to find ogre stories from online and offline sources,  conduct a reader’s theatre to read the stories,  answer direct and inferential questions from ogre stories,  identify vocabulary related to the theme from the stories,  create a vocabulary bank with new words from the stories,  work with peers to match the new words to their meaning,  work jointly with peers to fill in a word puzzle with vocabulary learnt from the theme,
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How can we read to get specific information from a text? 2. How do ogre stories differ from other stories?

strands.subStrand: Creative writing - Songs   Features  Aspects of language
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) outline the features of a song for information, b) compose a simple song related to the theme for effective communication, c) advocate for song writing as a way of recording indigenous knowledge.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  work jointly with peers to discuss the features of songs (e.g. lines, verses, refrain, and rhythm),  listen to varied songs related to the theme,  team up to compose simple songs on the theme,  share the songs with peers for review,  work with peers to record each other as they sing their own compositions,  discuss prominent song writers in the society and identify unique features about their compositions,  watch or listen to a song about a positive aspect of culture,  identify the message that the song communicates,  identify aspects of language use such as repetition, rhyme, imagery, and symbolism,
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How do we write an interesting song? 2. Why is writing important for indigenous knowledge?

strands.subStrand: Presentation skills – Songs   Intonation  Vocabulary building
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, learner should be able to: a) identify intonation used in speech for information, b) use acquired vocabulary to present a song, c) acknowledge the importance of audience awareness in presentation.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  take turns to read target words with correct intonation to bring out meaning,  work collaboratively to sing songs related to the theme,  identify vocabulary from the songs,  create a list of the vocabulary identified,  use the vocabulary to compose a song on the theme One Kenya, One Nation,  present the song and work jointly with peers to record the performances,  organise an indigenous languages festival and
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How can we make a presentation more appealing? 2. Why is correct intonation a key aspect in oral presentations?

strands.subStrand: Reading for information   Vocabulary building  Responding to questions
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify vocabulary used in texts for information, b) respond to texts on inter-ethnic cohesion for comprehension, c) embrace the need for inter-ethnic cohesion for better living.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  work with peers to find online or offline texts on inter-ethnic cohesion,  conduct a silent reading session on the texts,  make notes on key ideas expressed in the texts,  prepare a list of vocabulary identified from the texts read,  work with peers to identify the meaning of the vocabulary identified,  collaborate with peers to create mind maps on the vocabulary and generate other related words,  answer direct and inferential questions from the comprehension texts.
strands.inquiryQuestions: Why do we need to co-exist as a country despite our differences in culture?

strands.subStrand: Functional Writing – Posters
strands.outcomes: By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: a) identify features of a poster for information, b) design a poster on the theme for effective communication, c) acknowledge the role of posters in creating awareness for inter-ethnic cohesion.
strands.experiences: The learner is guided to:  surf the internet for sample posters on inter-ethnic cohesion,  work with peers to put together a collection of posters related to the theme from various sources,  identify features of an ideal poster,  work with peers to prepare a creative poster emphasising on the One Kenya, One Nation spirit,  share their posters with peers for review,  make adjustments on the posters based on feedback from peers,  display their refined posters in a class gallery,  publish or share the posters with friends and members of the community.
strands.inquiryQuestions: 1. How can posters be used to foster cohesion among people?
